slides.title: What is money?
slides.text: Money is what we use to buy things we want or need — like a snack, a toy, or a book.

slides.title: How do you get money?
slides.text: People earn money by working or doing helpful jobs — like completing chores!

slides.title: What does "saving" mean?
slides.text: Saving means keeping your money safe instead of spending it right away — like putting it in a piggy bank.

slides.title: Money can grow!
slides.text: If you plant a seed and take care of it, it grows into a big plant. Some ways of saving let your money grow bigger too, just like a seed!

slides.title: What does "spending" mean?
slides.text: Spending is using your money to get something you want right now, like a toy or an ice cream.

slides.title: What is a store?
slides.text: A store is a place that sells things for money. You give the store money, and the store gives you what you picked out.

slides.title: You can share money too
slides.text: Sometimes people use money to help others — like buying a gift for a friend, or giving to someone who needs it.

slides.title: Waiting for something special
slides.text: Sometimes the thing you want costs more than you have right now. Saving up a little at a time until you have enough is worth the wait.

slides.title: You get to choose!
slides.text: Every time you get money, you get to choose what to do with it: save it, spend it, or share it. There's no one right answer — it depends what you want most.

quiz.question: What can you use money for?
choices: Buying things you need
It has no use at all
quiz.explanation: That's right! Money lets us buy things like food, clothes, and toys.

quiz.question: Where is a safe place to keep money you're saving?
choices: Leave it on the ground
A piggy bank
quiz.explanation: A piggy bank (or a real bank!) keeps your saved money safe.

quiz.question: If you plant a seed and take care of it, what happens?
choices: It grows into a plant
It disappears forever
quiz.explanation: Just like a seed, money that's cared for the right way can grow too!

quiz.question: What happens when you use your money to buy a toy?
choices: That's called spending
That's called flying
quiz.explanation: Using money to get something now is called spending.

quiz.question: What is a store?
choices: A place that sells things for money
A place where money grows on trees
quiz.explanation: A store trades things you want for the money you give it.

quiz.question: If something costs more than you have right now, what can you do?
choices: Save up a little at a time until you have enough
It's impossible to ever get it
quiz.explanation: Saving up over time is how you afford things that cost more than you have today.

quiz.question: What are three things you can do with money?
choices: Save it, spend it, or share it
Only ever spend it
quiz.explanation: You always get to choose between saving, spending, or sharing your money.

slides.title: What is a bank?
slides.text: A bank is a safe place where people keep their money — like a giant, super-secure piggy bank.

slides.title: Saving for a goal
slides.text: Instead of spending money the moment you get it, you can save it up for something bigger you really want.

slides.title: What is interest?
slides.text: Some banks pay you a little extra money just for keeping your savings there. That extra bit is called interest — a small reward for saving.

slides.title: Wants vs. needs
slides.text: A need is something you must have, like food. A want is something nice to have, like a video game. Knowing the difference helps you spend wisely.

slides.title: Making a simple budget
slides.text: A budget is just a plan for your money — deciding ahead of time how much you'll save, spend, and maybe share, before you actually get it.

slides.title: Patience pays off
slides.text: Waiting a little longer before buying something — instead of grabbing it right away — often means you can afford something even better later.

slides.title: Comparing prices
slides.text: Smart shoppers check if the same thing costs less somewhere else before buying it. A few minutes of comparing can save a lot of points or money.

slides.title: Setting a savings goal
slides.text: Picking one specific thing to save for — and figuring out how many weeks of saving it'll take — makes saving feel a lot more real and exciting.

slides.title: What is a bank account?
slides.text: A bank account is like a digital piggy bank — the bank keeps track of exactly how much money you have, and you can check the balance any time.

slides.title: Watching your savings add up
slides.text: Writing down how much you've saved each week and adding it up is a simple way to actually see your money growing toward a goal.

quiz.question: What is a bank?
choices: A safe place to keep money
A place that takes your money away
quiz.explanation: Banks keep money safe, and some even pay you a little extra for saving with them.

quiz.question: If a bank gives you a little extra money just for saving, what's that called?
choices: A fine
Interest
quiz.explanation: Interest is like a small thank-you reward for keeping your money saved.

quiz.question: Which one is a "need"?
choices: A new video game
Food
quiz.explanation: Food is something you must have to live — that's a need, not just a want.

quiz.question: What's a smart way to get something big you really want?
choices: Save up for it over time
Never think about it
quiz.explanation: Saving a little at a time adds up to enough for bigger goals.

quiz.question: What's it called when you plan out ahead of time how you'll use your money?
choices: A budget
A trophy
quiz.explanation: A budget is simply a plan for saving, spending, and sharing your money.

quiz.question: Why might someone check prices in more than one place before buying?
choices: To find the same thing for less
It never makes a difference
quiz.explanation: Comparing prices can help you find a better deal and save the rest.

quiz.question: What can help make a savings goal feel more real?
choices: Picking one specific thing to save for
Never deciding what you're saving for
quiz.explanation: A clear, specific goal makes it much easier to stay motivated while saving.

quiz.question: What is a bank account?
choices: A way the bank keeps track of exactly how much money you have
A type of toy
quiz.explanation: A bank account tracks your balance so you always know how much you've saved.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to write down and add up your savings each week?
choices: You can actually see your money growing toward your goal
It has no real purpose
quiz.explanation: Tracking your savings makes progress toward a goal feel real and motivating.

slides.title: What is investing?
slides.text: Investing means using your money to buy a small piece of something — like a company — hoping it grows in value over time.

slides.title: What is a stock?
slides.text: A stock is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your tiny piece can become worth more.

slides.title: Risk and reward
slides.text: Investments can go up AND down in value. Taking on some risk is part of how investing can lead to bigger rewards over time.

slides.title: The power of time
slides.text: The earlier you start investing — even with a small amount — the more time your money has to grow. Time is a young investor's biggest advantage.

slides.title: What is compound interest?
slides.text: Compound interest means you earn money not just on what you put in, but also on the money it already earned before. It's growth building on growth.

slides.title: Short-term vs. long-term goals
slides.text: Money you need soon (like next month) is usually better off saved, not invested. Money you won't need for many years has more room to ride out an investment's ups and downs.

slides.title: What is a "loss"?
slides.text: Sometimes an investment's value drops for a while — that's a loss on paper. It only becomes a real loss if you sell while it's down instead of waiting for it to recover.

slides.title: Investing vs. an allowance
slides.text: An allowance is money you're simply given. Investing is different — it's money you put to work, hoping it grows into more than you started with.

slides.title: Investing a little, regularly
slides.text: Instead of investing one big amount all at once, some people invest a smaller amount on a regular schedule — like monthly. This is sometimes called dollar-cost averaging, and it smooths out the ups and downs.

slides.title: What is a brokerage account?
slides.text: A brokerage account is where you actually buy and hold investments like stocks — different from a regular bank account, which just holds cash.

quiz.question: What does "investing" mean?
choices: Using money to buy something that can grow in value
Hiding money so nobody can find it
quiz.explanation: Investing puts your money to work, hoping it grows over time.

quiz.question: What is a stock?
choices: A type of bank account
A small piece of ownership in a company
quiz.explanation: Owning a stock means owning a tiny slice of that company.

quiz.question: True or False: Investments only ever go up in value.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: Investments can go up and down — that ups-and-downs risk is part of how investing works.

quiz.question: Why is starting young such a big advantage for investing?
choices: More time for your money to grow
It isn't actually an advantage
quiz.explanation: The earlier you start, the more time your money has to grow bigger.

quiz.question: If a company you own a tiny piece of grows and does well, what usually happens to your piece?
choices: It becomes worth more
It disappears
quiz.explanation: When a company grows in value, the pieces of it people own — including yours — tend to grow in value too.

quiz.question: What does "compound interest" mean?
choices: You earn money on your original money AND on what it already earned
You only ever earn money once
quiz.explanation: Compounding is growth building on top of previous growth — it speeds up over time.

quiz.question: An investment drops in value for a while, but you leave it alone and it recovers later. Was that a real loss?
choices: No — it only becomes a real loss if you sell while it's down
Yes, any drop is a permanent loss
quiz.explanation: A drop is just 'on paper' until you actually sell — patience often lets it recover.

quiz.question: What is "dollar-cost averaging"?
choices: Investing a smaller amount regularly instead of all at once
Only ever investing in dollar bills
quiz.explanation: Investing smaller amounts on a schedule helps smooth out an investment's ups and downs.

quiz.question: What is a brokerage account used for?
choices: Actually buying and holding investments like stocks
Only storing cash, like a regular bank account
quiz.explanation: A brokerage account is specifically where investments are bought and held.

slides.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
slides.text: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments instead of just one, so one bad outcome doesn't wipe you out.

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text: Instead of picking one company, an index fund lets you own a tiny piece of hundreds of companies at once — an easy way to diversify.

slides.title: Inflation: the silent thief
slides.text: Prices tend to rise over time. Money that just sits still loses buying power. Investing is one way to try to grow money faster than inflation shrinks it.

slides.title: Long-term thinking beats quick wins
slides.text: Investors who stay patient through ups and downs, over years or decades, tend to do far better than those chasing quick trades.

slides.title: Debt works the opposite way
slides.text: Investing grows money for you over time. Borrowing money (debt) usually costs you extra over time through interest — it's compounding working against you instead of for you.

slides.title: Retirement accounts, simplified
slides.text: Many workplaces offer special accounts (like a 401(k) or an IRA in the US) built for long-term investing, often with tax advantages. They're designed to be left alone for decades.

slides.title: Getting started today
slides.text: Modern investing apps and custodial accounts have made it easier than ever for a teenager to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help.

slides.title: The Rule of 72
slides.text: A quick trick: divide 72 by your investment's yearly growth rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 8% growth, that's roughly 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years to double.

slides.title: Bull markets and bear markets
slides.text: A 'bull market' is a stretch of time when prices are generally rising. A 'bear market' is a stretch when prices are generally falling. Both are completely normal parts of a long investing journey.

slides.title: A brief word on taxes
slides.text: In many places, profit made from selling an investment can be taxed — often called a capital gains tax. It's a real cost worth knowing about, even though the details vary a lot by country.

quiz.question: What does "diversification" mean?
choices: Putting all your money into one company
Spreading your money across many different investments
quiz.explanation: Diversification helps protect you — one investment doing poorly doesn't sink everything.

quiz.question: What is an index fund?
choices: A fund that owns tiny pieces of hundreds of companies at once
A savings account with no interest
quiz.explanation: Index funds are a simple way to diversify without picking individual companies yourself.

quiz.question: What is inflation?
choices: Prices rising over time, which reduces what your money can buy
A type of investment account
quiz.explanation: Inflation quietly erodes the value of money that just sits still.

quiz.question: True or False: Reacting quickly to every market dip usually leads to better long-term results.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: Panicking over short-term dips often hurts long-term investors more than it helps.

quiz.question: What's one key benefit of starting to invest as a teenager instead of waiting until your 30s?
choices: Many more years for compound growth
No real benefit either way
quiz.explanation: Starting early gives your money decades more time to compound.

quiz.question: How is borrowing money (debt) different from investing?
choices: Debt usually costs you extra over time instead of growing your money
They work exactly the same way
quiz.explanation: Interest on debt compounds against you, while investing aims to compound growth for you.

quiz.question: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years would it take money to double at 9% yearly growth?
choices: About 8 years
About 50 years
quiz.explanation: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 — a handy shortcut for estimating doubling time.

quiz.question: What is a "bear market"?
choices: A stretch of time when prices are generally falling
A market that only sells stuffed animals
quiz.explanation: A bear market describes a generally declining stretch of prices — a normal part of investing.

quiz.question: What is a capital gains tax generally applied to?
choices: Profit made from selling an investment
Every dollar you ever save
quiz.explanation: Capital gains tax typically applies to the profit from selling an investment, not savings itself.

slides.title: Meet AI!
slides.text: AI is a computer helper. It can listen to you and talk back — kind of like a friendly robot voice.

slides.title: Ask it something!
slides.text: Some speakers and toys can answer your questions or play your favorite song when you ask them out loud.

slides.title: A person built it
slides.text: AI doesn't just appear out of nowhere — clever people built it to help us, just like someone built your favorite toy.

slides.title: AI doesn't have real feelings
slides.text: Even when AI talks in a friendly voice, it can't really feel happy, sad, or love you the way a person or a pet can.

slides.title: AI can help make things
slides.text: Some AI can help draw a silly picture or make up a story when you ask it to — like a helper for making fun stuff.

slides.title: AI isn't always right
slides.text: Sometimes AI gets confused and gives a silly or wrong answer — it's still learning, just like you are!

slides.title: AI can make music too
slides.text: Some AI can put sounds together to make a little tune, kind of like how it can help draw a picture.

slides.title: AI shows up in surprising places
slides.text: AI can help some toy cars drive themselves around a track, or help a game character know where to move next.

slides.title: Ask a grown-up first
slides.text: If you want to use an AI toy or app, or you're not sure about something it says, always check with a grown-up first.

quiz.question: What is AI?
choices: A kind of animal
A computer helper that can listen and talk
quiz.explanation: AI is a computer helper, not a living creature.

quiz.question: Can AI feel happy or sad, like you can?
choices: No, it can't really feel things
Yes, exactly like a person
quiz.explanation: AI can sound friendly, but it doesn't truly feel emotions.

quiz.question: Who makes AI?
choices: People who build it
It just appears by itself
quiz.explanation: People build AI on purpose, the same way people build toys and apps.

quiz.question: If AI gives a silly or wrong answer, what does that mean?
choices: It's always right, no matter what
It's not perfect — it's still learning
quiz.explanation: AI can make mistakes, just like anyone still learning something new.

quiz.question: If you want to use an AI toy or app, what should you do first?
choices: Check with a grown-up
Just use it secretly
quiz.explanation: A grown-up can help make sure it's safe and okay to use.

quiz.question: Can AI help make a little piece of music?
choices: Yes, it can put sounds together
No, AI can never make sounds
quiz.explanation: AI can help create sounds and music, similar to how it can help draw pictures.

quiz.question: Where might AI show up in a toy?
choices: Helping a toy car steer itself around a track
AI never shows up in any toy
quiz.explanation: AI can be built into toys, like helping a toy car or game character move on its own.

slides.title: AI learns from examples
slides.text: Instead of being told exact rules, AI often learns by looking at thousands (or millions!) of examples and finding patterns in them.

slides.title: Where you already see AI
slides.text: Video game characters that react to you, apps that recommend videos you might like, and voice assistants all use AI.

slides.title: Finding patterns
slides.text: If AI sees enough pictures of dogs, it starts noticing patterns — like "dogs usually have four legs and fur" — and uses that to guess.

slides.title: AI can make mistakes
slides.text: Because AI learns from patterns, it can sometimes get things wrong — especially with something unusual it hasn't seen much before.

slides.title: AI vs. your brain
slides.text: Your brain can understand feelings, come up with brand-new ideas, and truly care about people. AI is very good at specific tasks, but it doesn't understand things the way you do.

slides.title: Being a smart AI user
slides.text: Just because AI says something doesn't mean it's true. Smart AI users double-check important information instead of believing everything right away.

slides.title: Robots vs. AI
slides.text: A robot is a physical machine. AI is the 'smart' software that can control a robot — or can run inside a phone or computer with no robot body at all.

slides.title: AI helps you search
slides.text: When you search for something online, AI often helps decide which results are most likely to actually answer your question.

slides.title: People see AI differently
slides.text: Some people are really excited about AI and what it can do. Others feel worried about it. Both views are worth listening to — AI is still a new, changing technology.

quiz.question: How does AI usually learn to recognize things?
choices: By looking at lots of examples and finding patterns
By reading a single instruction book once
quiz.explanation: AI typically learns from huge numbers of examples, not a short list of rules.

quiz.question: True or False: AI never makes mistakes.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: AI can definitely get things wrong, especially with unusual situations.

quiz.question: What's something your brain can do that AI really can't?
choices: Truly understand feelings and have original ideas
Recognize a picture of a dog
quiz.explanation: AI can recognize patterns well, but it doesn't truly feel or originate ideas the way you do.

quiz.question: If an app recommends a video you might like, what is it doing?
choices: Using patterns from what you've watched before
Reading your mind
quiz.explanation: Recommendation systems use patterns in your past choices to guess what you'll like.

quiz.question: Is a robot the same thing as AI?
choices: Yes, they're identical
No — a robot is a machine; AI is the smart software
quiz.explanation: AI can control a robot, but AI can also run with no robot body at all, like inside an app.

quiz.question: What should you do if AI tells you something you're not sure is true?
choices: Double-check it
Always assume it's correct
quiz.explanation: Checking important facts is a great habit, especially with AI answers.

quiz.question: What does AI often help with when you search online?
choices: Deciding which results best answer your question
Nothing — search results are picked at random
quiz.explanation: AI helps rank and select search results that are likely to match what you're looking for.

quiz.question: Do all people feel the same way about AI?
choices: No, some are excited and some are worried
Yes, everyone agrees completely
quiz.explanation: AI is a new, changing technology, and people reasonably have different views about it.

slides.title: Training data
slides.text: AI systems are "trained" on huge amounts of data — text, images, or numbers — that teach the AI the patterns it's meant to learn.

slides.title: Prediction, not real understanding
slides.text: Many AI tools, like chatbots, work by predicting the most likely next word or answer based on patterns — not by truly understanding meaning the way a person does.

slides.title: AI can be biased
slides.text: If the data used to train an AI contains unfair patterns, the AI can repeat those unfair patterns too. This is called bias, and it's a real challenge engineers work hard to fix.

slides.title: Generative AI
slides.text: Some AI can create brand-new text, images, or music by combining patterns it learned — this is called generative AI, and it powers many chatbots and art generators.

slides.title: AI and privacy
slides.text: AI tools often need data to work well. Being thoughtful about what personal information you share with an AI app matters, just like with any app.

slides.title: Fact-checking AI answers
slides.text: AI can sound very confident even when it's wrong — sometimes called a "hallucination." Always double-check important facts from a trusted source.

slides.title: AI's growing role
slides.text: AI already helps translate languages, spot diseases in medical scans, and recommend what you watch or read — and its role keeps growing.

slides.title: AI working with people
slides.text: In many fields, AI is a tool that works alongside a person — helping a doctor spot something on a scan faster, for example — rather than fully replacing their judgment.

slides.title: AI keeps changing
slides.text: AI systems get updated and retrained over time, so an AI tool from a year ago might behave quite differently — hopefully better — today.

quiz.question: What is "training data"?
choices: The examples used to teach an AI its patterns
A type of computer chip
quiz.explanation: Training data is what an AI studies to learn the patterns it uses later.

quiz.question: Do chatbots truly "understand" language the way people do?
choices: Yes, exactly the same way
No — they mostly predict likely next words based on patterns
quiz.explanation: Chatbots are pattern-predictors, not conscious understanders of meaning.

quiz.question: What does it mean if an AI is "biased"?
choices: It repeats unfair patterns from the data it learned from
It always tells the truth
quiz.explanation: Bias in training data can show up as unfair patterns in what the AI produces.

quiz.question: What is generative AI?
choices: AI that can create new text, images, or other content
AI that can only sort numbers
quiz.explanation: Generative AI produces brand-new content by combining patterns it learned.

quiz.question: What is it called when AI confidently states something that's false?
choices: A hallucination
A firewall
quiz.explanation: A "hallucination" is AI stating something confidently that just isn't true.

quiz.question: Why should you be careful about what personal info you share with AI apps?
choices: That data might be stored or used by the app
It has no effect on anything
quiz.explanation: Just like any app, what you share with an AI tool can be stored or used elsewhere.

quiz.question: Which is a genuinely helpful real-world use of AI today?
choices: Translating languages
Doing all your homework so you learn nothing
quiz.explanation: Translation, medical scan analysis, and recommendations are real, helpful AI uses.

quiz.question: In many fields, how does AI typically work alongside people?
choices: As a helpful tool, not a full replacement for their judgment
By completely taking over every decision
quiz.explanation: AI often assists a person's work rather than fully replacing their judgment.

quiz.question: Does an AI tool stay exactly the same forever once it's released?
choices: No, it often gets updated and retrained over time
Yes, it never changes at all
quiz.explanation: AI systems are commonly updated, so their behavior can change over time.

slides.title: Neural networks, simplified
slides.text: Many modern AI systems are loosely inspired by how brain cells connect — layers of simple math functions combining to recognize very complex patterns.

slides.title: Large language models
slides.text: Chatbots you may have used are often "large language models" trained on enormous amounts of text to predict likely, coherent responses.

slides.title: Bias and fairness
slides.text: Because AI learns from real-world data, it can inherit real-world unfairness, like reflecting stereotypes. Researchers actively study how to detect and reduce this.

slides.title: Deepfakes and misinformation
slides.text: AI can now generate very convincing fake images, video, or audio. Learning to question what you see online is a genuinely important skill now.

slides.title: AI and jobs
slides.text: AI is changing many jobs — automating some repetitive tasks while creating new kinds of work. Understanding AI, rather than fearing it, is a real advantage for your future.

slides.title: Using AI responsibly for school
slides.text: AI can be a great study partner for explaining concepts, but relying on it to do your thinking for you weakens the exact skills you're in school to build.

slides.title: Data and consent
slides.text: Many AI systems are trained on massive datasets pulled from the internet, which raises real questions about consent and ownership that society is still working out.

slides.title: Why understanding AI matters for you
slides.text: Whatever career you choose, AI will likely touch it. Understanding the basics now — not just using AI, but roughly how it works and where it fails — is a genuine head start.

slides.title: AI and energy use
slides.text: Training very large AI models takes a significant amount of computing power and electricity — an environmental cost that researchers and companies are actively working to reduce.

slides.title: New rules for AI
slides.text: Governments around the world are starting to write laws and regulations about how AI can be built and used — an evolving area, similar to how early internet and privacy laws once developed.

quiz.question: What is a "large language model"?
choices: An AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict likely responses
A physical robot used in factories
quiz.explanation: LLMs are trained on massive text datasets to generate likely, coherent responses.

quiz.question: True or False: AI is completely free of bias since it's "just math."
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: AI can absolutely inherit bias from the data it was trained on.

quiz.question: What is a "deepfake"?
choices: A realistic AI-generated fake image, video, or audio clip
A very deep ocean AI-powered submarine
quiz.explanation: Deepfakes are convincing AI-generated fakes, which is why questioning sources online matters.

quiz.question: Why is it risky to let AI fully do your homework for you?
choices: It weakens the exact skills you're meant to be building
There is no risk at all
quiz.explanation: Using AI as a shortcut around learning undermines the point of doing the work.

quiz.question: What is one real way AI is affecting the job market?
choices: Automating some tasks while creating new kinds of work
It has no effect on jobs whatsoever
quiz.explanation: AI both removes and creates work — understanding it is an advantage either way.

quiz.question: What ethical question does training AI on scraped internet data raise?
choices: Consent and ownership of that data
Whether the internet uses too much electricity
quiz.explanation: Whether creators consented to their work being used for AI training is a live debate.

quiz.question: What's a smart way to use AI as a student?
choices: As a study aid to help understand concepts
As a total replacement for your own thinking
quiz.explanation: AI works best as a tool that supports your learning, not one that replaces it.

quiz.question: Neural networks are loosely inspired by what?
choices: How brain cells connect to each other
How electricity flows through a wall socket
quiz.explanation: The "neural" in neural networks nods to this loose inspiration from the brain.

quiz.question: Why does training large AI models raise environmental concerns?
choices: It takes significant computing power and electricity
AI models are grown from actual trees
quiz.explanation: Large-scale AI training has a real energy cost that's an active area of research to reduce.

quiz.question: What are governments starting to do about AI?
choices: Write laws and regulations about how it can be built and used
Nothing at all, anywhere
quiz.explanation: AI regulation is an evolving area as governments respond to the technology's growth.

slides.title: What is a lemonade stand?
slides.text: A lemonade stand is a tiny business — you make something (lemonade!) and sell it to people who want to buy it.

slides.title: What is trading?
slides.text: Trading means giving someone something they want, and getting something you want back — like a coin for a cup of lemonade.

slides.title: Where ideas come from
slides.text: A business often starts with a simple idea — like noticing people get thirsty and thinking, 'I could sell them a cold drink!'

slides.title: Who is a customer?
slides.text: A customer is someone who buys what you're selling. Being friendly and helpful makes customers want to come back.

slides.title: You can make things too!
slides.text: Drawing pictures, making bracelets, or baking cookies to share or sell are all little ways of being an entrepreneur — someone who makes and offers things.

slides.title: It takes effort
slides.text: Making a lemonade stand work takes real effort — squeezing lemons, making a sign, and standing there smiling at customers!

slides.title: Making something to sell
slides.text: Before you can sell something, you have to make it first — like squeezing the lemons and mixing in sugar and water to actually make the lemonade.

slides.title: A happy customer comes back
slides.text: When a customer really likes what you sold them, they often want to come back and buy from you again.

quiz.question: What is a lemonade stand?
choices: A tiny business selling lemonade
A place to take a nap
quiz.explanation: A lemonade stand is a simple, real example of running a tiny business.

quiz.question: What is a customer?
choices: Someone who buys what you're selling
A type of lemon
quiz.explanation: Customers are the people who buy from your business.

quiz.question: What happens when you trade?
choices: You give something and get something back
Nothing happens at all
quiz.explanation: Trading is a fair exchange — giving something, getting something back.

quiz.question: Where do business ideas often come from?
choices: Noticing something people want or need
They only come from grown-ups, never kids
quiz.explanation: Great business ideas often start by noticing a want or need, like being thirsty on a hot day.

quiz.question: Does running a lemonade stand take effort?
choices: Yes, it takes real work
No, it happens by itself
quiz.explanation: From squeezing lemons to making a sign, a lemonade stand takes real effort to run.

quiz.question: What has to happen before you can sell something?
choices: You have to make it first
You can sell it before it exists
quiz.explanation: Making the lemonade comes before selling it — you need something real to offer.

quiz.question: What often happens when a customer really likes what you sold them?
choices: They want to come back and buy again
They never think about it again
quiz.explanation: A happy customer is likely to return, which helps a little business keep going.

slides.title: Spotting a problem to solve
slides.text: Good business ideas often start by spotting a problem — like 'nobody sells cold water at the park' — and figuring out how to fix it.

slides.title: Cost vs. price
slides.text: Cost is what it takes to make something (like lemons and sugar). Price is what you charge someone to buy it. The difference is your profit.

slides.title: A simple plan
slides.text: Before starting, it helps to plan: what will you sell, how much will it cost to make, and how much will you charge?

slides.title: Good customer service
slides.text: Being friendly, honest, and helpful makes people want to buy from you again — and tell their friends about you too.

slides.title: Telling people about it
slides.text: Even a great product needs people to know it exists! A colorful sign or telling your neighbors is a simple form of marketing.

slides.title: Keeping track
slides.text: Writing down what you spent and what you earned helps you see if your little business is actually making money.

slides.title: Trying again if it doesn't work
slides.text: If a business idea doesn't work the first time, entrepreneurs often tweak it and try again instead of giving up.

slides.title: Making your product special
slides.text: Adding something unique — like a fun flavor of lemonade nobody else has — can make customers pick your stand over anyone else's.

slides.title: Planning your day
slides.text: Deciding when to open your stand, how much lemonade to make, and what supplies you need ahead of time helps the whole day run more smoothly.

quiz.question: What does it mean to "spot a problem" for a business idea?
choices: Noticing something people need that isn't available
Finding a hole in your sock
quiz.explanation: Great business ideas often start by noticing a real need that isn't being met.

quiz.question: What is "profit"?
choices: The difference between what something costs to make and its price
Another word for a customer
quiz.explanation: Profit is what's left over after you subtract the cost from the price you charged.

quiz.question: Why is a simple plan helpful before starting a business?
choices: It helps you figure out what to sell and for how much
Plans are only for grown-ups
quiz.explanation: A simple plan helps you think through what you'll sell, what it costs, and what to charge.

quiz.question: Why does good customer service matter?
choices: It makes customers want to come back and tell friends
It has no real effect on a business
quiz.explanation: Friendly, helpful service builds trust and brings customers back.

quiz.question: What is marketing, in simple terms?
choices: Telling people about what you're selling
Counting your money at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Marketing is simply letting people know your product or service exists.

quiz.question: If a business idea doesn't work at first, what do entrepreneurs usually do?
choices: Tweak the idea and try again
Never attempt anything again
quiz.explanation: Adjusting and retrying is a normal, healthy part of entrepreneurship.

quiz.question: How can making your product special help a business?
choices: It can make customers pick you over other sellers
It never makes any difference
quiz.explanation: Something unique about your product gives customers a reason to choose you.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to plan your day before opening a stand?
choices: It helps the whole day run more smoothly
Planning ahead never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Knowing what supplies and timing you need ahead of time avoids scrambling later.

slides.title: Profit and loss
slides.text: If you earn more than you spend, that's a profit. If you spend more than you earn, that's a loss. Tracking both helps a business survive.

slides.title: Knowing your customer
slides.text: Successful businesses understand who they're selling to — what that person likes, needs, and is willing to pay for.

slides.title: Teamwork in business
slides.text: Many businesses run better with a team — different people handling different jobs, like making the product, selling it, and managing money.

slides.title: Taking a smart risk
slides.text: Starting a business always involves some risk — it might not work. Smart entrepreneurs take risks they can afford, not risks that could ruin them.

slides.title: Reinvesting in growth
slides.text: Instead of spending all the profit right away, many entrepreneurs put some of it back into the business — better supplies, a nicer sign, more inventory.

slides.title: Standing out from competitors
slides.text: If other people sell something similar, a business needs a reason customers should pick them — better quality, price, or service.

slides.title: Word of mouth
slides.text: Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful (and free!) ways a small business grows.

slides.title: Building a name people remember
slides.text: A consistent name, look, or feel for your business — sometimes called a brand — helps customers recognize and trust you again next time.

slides.title: Selling online with help
slides.text: With a parent's help, some young entrepreneurs sell crafts or art through simple online marketplaces, reaching far more people than a stand on the street.

quiz.question: What is a "loss" in business?
choices: Spending more than you earn
Earning more than you spend
quiz.explanation: A loss happens when costs are higher than what the business earns.

quiz.question: Why does it help to understand your customer?
choices: So you can offer what they actually want and can afford
It doesn't matter who buys your product
quiz.explanation: Knowing your customer helps you shape a product or service they'll actually want.

quiz.question: What does "reinvesting" mean?
choices: Putting some profit back into growing the business
Spending every bit of profit immediately
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting profit helps a business grow bigger and stronger over time.

quiz.question: What is a "smart risk" in business?
choices: A risk you can afford, taken thoughtfully
Any risk at all, no matter the size
quiz.explanation: Smart entrepreneurs weigh risks carefully instead of risking everything blindly.

quiz.question: Why might a business need to "stand out" from competitors?
choices: So customers have a reason to choose them specifically
Standing out never matters in business
quiz.explanation: If others sell something similar, standing out gives customers a reason to pick you.

quiz.question: What is "word of mouth"?
choices: Happy customers telling other people about a business
A type of advertisement you have to pay a lot for
quiz.explanation: Word of mouth is free, powerful marketing that comes from satisfied customers.

quiz.question: What is a "brand"?
choices: A consistent name or look that helps customers recognize a business
A random word with no meaning
quiz.explanation: A recognizable brand builds trust and makes customers more likely to return.

quiz.question: How might a young entrepreneur reach more customers than a street stand?
choices: Selling online with a parent's help
It's impossible to ever reach more people
quiz.explanation: Online marketplaces, used with a parent's guidance, can reach far more people than a physical stand.

slides.title: What is a business plan?
slides.text: A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, how it'll make money, and what it needs to get started — a roadmap for turning an idea into reality.

slides.title: Startup vs. small business
slides.text: A small business often grows steadily and stays similar in size. A startup usually aims to grow very fast, often testing a new idea that hasn't been proven yet.

slides.title: Where funding comes from
slides.text: Businesses can be funded with personal savings, loans, or investors who give money in exchange for a share of future profits or ownership.

slides.title: What does "scaling" mean?
slides.text: Scaling means growing a business to serve many more customers without everything becoming proportionally more expensive or difficult to manage.

slides.title: Failure is part of the process
slides.text: Many successful entrepreneurs failed at a first (or second, or third) attempt. Learning from what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt succeed.

slides.title: Ethics in business
slides.text: Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers, treating employees fairly, and not cutting corners just to make a quick profit.

slides.title: Solving a real problem
slides.text: The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine problem for people — not just chase a trend that might fade quickly.

slides.title: Resilience and persistence
slides.text: Markets change, plans fail, and competitors appear. Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback.

slides.title: Businesses that also help others
slides.text: Some entrepreneurs build 'social enterprises' — businesses designed to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem, not purely for profit.

slides.title: Measuring success beyond money
slides.text: Revenue matters, but many entrepreneurs also track customer satisfaction, repeat business, and real-world impact as signs their business is genuinely succeeding.

quiz.question: What is a business plan?
choices: A roadmap covering what a business will sell, who it's for, and how it makes money
A legal document required only for huge companies
quiz.explanation: A business plan turns a rough idea into a structured, actionable roadmap.

quiz.question: How does a startup typically differ from a small business?
choices: A startup usually aims to grow very fast with an unproven idea
There is no real difference between them
quiz.explanation: Startups often chase fast, unproven growth; small businesses often grow more steadily.

quiz.question: What might an investor get in exchange for funding a business?
choices: A share of future profits or ownership
Nothing at all, ever
quiz.explanation: Investors typically fund a business in exchange for equity or a share of future returns.

quiz.question: What does "scaling" a business mean?
choices: Growing to serve many more customers without costs exploding proportionally
Weighing the business on a scale
quiz.explanation: Scaling is about growing efficiently, not just growing bigger at any cost.

quiz.question: Why do many successful entrepreneurs talk openly about past failures?
choices: Learning from what went wrong often shapes what succeeds next
Failure has no useful lessons at all
quiz.explanation: Failure is frequently a genuine part of the path to eventual success.

quiz.question: Why does ethical behavior matter for long-term business success?
choices: Cutting corners for quick profit tends to damage trust over time
Ethics have no real impact on whether a business succeeds
quiz.explanation: Businesses built on trust and fairness tend to last longer than ones that cut corners.

quiz.question: What tends to make a business durable over the long run?
choices: Solving a genuine, ongoing problem for people
Only ever chasing whatever trend is popular right now
quiz.explanation: Businesses solving real, lasting problems tend to outlast those chasing short-lived trends.

quiz.question: What is a "social enterprise"?
choices: A business built to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem
A business that only exists on social media
quiz.explanation: Social enterprises intentionally pursue impact alongside profit.

quiz.question: Besides revenue, what else might an entrepreneur track as a sign of success?
choices: Customer satisfaction and real-world impact
Nothing else is ever worth tracking
quiz.explanation: Many entrepreneurs value signs of genuine success beyond just the money earned.

slides.title: Why do we ask "why"?
slides.text: Asking 'why' helps you understand things better — like why the sky looks blue, or why ice melts in the sun.

slides.title: Same or different?
slides.text: Looking closely at two things and noticing how they're the same or different is a great thinking skill — like comparing two toys.

slides.title: Real or pretend?
slides.text: A cartoon dragon breathing fire is pretend. A real dog barking is real. Telling the difference is an important thinking skill.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Taking a moment to think before doing something — like before grabbing a toy from a friend — often leads to a better choice.

slides.title: Looking for clues
slides.text: If your shoes are wet, you can think about clues to figure out why — did it rain? Did you step in a puddle?

slides.title: It's okay to ask questions
slides.text: If something doesn't make sense, asking a question is smart — not silly. Good thinkers ask lots of questions.

slides.title: Sorting things into groups
slides.text: Putting toys into groups — like all the red ones together, or all the round ones together — is a first step toward organized thinking.

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.text: Looking at a pattern like circle, square, circle, square and figuring out what comes next is a fun way to practice thinking ahead.

quiz.question: Why is asking "why" a good habit?
choices: It helps you understand things better
It never helps at all
quiz.explanation: Asking "why" is one of the best ways to understand the world around you.

quiz.question: A cartoon dragon breathing fire — is that real or pretend?
choices: Pretend
Real
quiz.explanation: Cartoons show pretend things, even if they look exciting.

quiz.question: What can help you make a better choice?
choices: Thinking for a moment before acting
Acting right away without thinking at all
quiz.explanation: A moment of thought before acting often leads to a better decision.

quiz.question: If your shoes are wet, what could you do to figure out why?
choices: Look for clues, like whether it rained
There's no way to ever know
quiz.explanation: Looking for clues is exactly how good thinkers solve little mysteries.

quiz.question: Is it okay to ask a question when something doesn't make sense?
choices: Yes, asking questions is smart
No, you should never ask questions
quiz.explanation: Asking questions is a sign of a curious, careful thinker.

quiz.question: What is a good first step toward organized thinking?
choices: Sorting things into groups
Mixing everything together randomly
quiz.explanation: Grouping similar things together is a simple, useful thinking skill.

quiz.question: In the pattern circle, square, circle, square — what comes next?
choices: Circle
A triangle
quiz.explanation: The pattern repeats circle then square, so a circle comes next.

slides.title: Fact vs. opinion
slides.text: A fact is something that's true and can be checked, like 'the sun is hot.' An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, like 'summer is the best season.'

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Instead of just accepting an answer, good thinkers ask follow-up questions like 'how do you know that?' or 'is there another way to look at this?'

slides.title: More than one answer
slides.text: Some questions have more than one reasonable answer. Thinking about different possibilities, not just the first idea, leads to better decisions.

slides.title: Don't believe everything right away
slides.text: Just because something is written down, said out loud, or shown online doesn't automatically make it true.

slides.title: Checking with a trusted source
slides.text: If you're not sure whether something is true, checking with a grown-up, a book, or a trusted website is a smart next step.

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: Thinking about why something happened — the cause — and what happened because of it — the effect — helps you understand the world more clearly.

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: If new information shows your first idea was wrong, a good thinker isn't afraid to change their mind.

slides.title: Being a detective
slides.text: A good detective gathers several clues before deciding what happened, instead of guessing after just one clue. Thinking works the same way.

slides.title: It's okay to disagree
slides.text: Two people can look at the same thing and see it differently. Disagreeing with a friend — respectfully — doesn't mean the friendship is in trouble.

quiz.question: What is a "fact"?
choices: Something true that can be checked
Whatever someone happens to feel
quiz.explanation: Facts are checkable and true, unlike opinions, which are personal views.

quiz.question: What is an "opinion"?
choices: What someone thinks or feels
Something that can be proven true or false
quiz.explanation: Opinions are personal views — they can differ from person to person.

quiz.question: If someone tells you something surprising, what's a smart response?
choices: Ask "how do you know that?"
Believe it immediately with no questions
quiz.explanation: Asking follow-up questions is a great way to think critically about new information.

quiz.question: Does everything you read online automatically become true?
choices: No, it should be checked
Yes, if it's written down it's always true
quiz.explanation: Being written or posted online doesn't make something automatically true.

quiz.question: What does "cause and effect" mean?
choices: Understanding why something happened and what resulted from it
A game with no real meaning
quiz.explanation: Cause and effect helps you connect why something happened to what happened next.

quiz.question: Is it okay to change your mind if you learn new information?
choices: Yes, that's what good thinkers do
No, you should never change your mind
quiz.explanation: Updating your thinking based on new evidence is a sign of strong critical thinking.

quiz.question: What does a good detective do before deciding what happened?
choices: Gathers several clues first
Guesses after just one clue
quiz.explanation: Good thinking, like good detective work, weighs multiple clues before concluding.

quiz.question: Does disagreeing with a friend mean the friendship is in trouble?
choices: No, respectful disagreement is normal
Yes, friends must always agree on everything
quiz.explanation: People can see things differently and still be good friends.

slides.title: Evaluating evidence
slides.text: Before believing a claim, it helps to ask: what evidence supports it? Is the evidence strong, weak, or missing entirely?

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something believed without proof. Noticing hidden assumptions in an argument helps you judge whether it actually holds up.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Just because two things happen around the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn.

slides.title: Considering other perspectives
slides.text: Understanding how a situation looks from someone else's point of view often reveals things your own perspective alone would miss.

slides.title: Weighing both sides
slides.text: On a genuinely debatable topic, looking fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides — before forming an opinion — leads to more solid conclusions.

slides.title: Defining the real problem
slides.text: Sometimes what looks like the problem is actually just a symptom of a different, deeper problem. Defining the real issue is the first step to solving it well.

slides.title: Checking the source
slides.text: Who is saying this, and why? A source with something to gain from you believing a claim deserves a closer, more careful look.

slides.title: Setting a goal and checking progress
slides.text: Deciding what you're aiming for, then regularly checking whether your approach is actually getting you closer, keeps effort from being wasted.

slides.title: Averages can mislead
slides.text: An average can hide a lot — a class 'average score' of 75% might mean everyone scored near 75%, or it might mean half scored 100% and half scored 50%.

quiz.question: What should you check before believing a claim?
choices: What evidence actually supports it
Nothing — just believe confident-sounding claims
quiz.explanation: Strong claims deserve strong evidence — checking for it is a core critical thinking skill.

quiz.question: What is an "assumption"?
choices: Something believed without proof
A fact that has been proven true
quiz.explanation: Assumptions are unproven beliefs that can weaken an argument if left unchecked.

quiz.question: Does one thing happening alongside another always mean it caused it?
choices: No — correlation isn't the same as causation
Yes, if two things happen together one always causes the other
quiz.explanation: Two things happening together doesn't prove one caused the other.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to consider other people's perspectives?
choices: It can reveal things your own viewpoint alone would miss
Other perspectives are never worth considering
quiz.explanation: Different viewpoints often surface details a single perspective would overlook.

quiz.question: Why does it matter who is making a claim, and why?
choices: A source with something to gain deserves closer scrutiny
The source of a claim never matters
quiz.explanation: Considering a source's motives is part of evaluating how trustworthy a claim is.

quiz.question: What does "defining the real problem" mean?
choices: Making sure you're solving the actual issue, not just a symptom of it
Skipping straight to a solution without thinking
quiz.explanation: Solving the wrong problem — even solving it well — doesn't actually help.

quiz.question: Why is checking progress toward a goal useful?
choices: It keeps effort from being wasted on the wrong approach
Checking progress never matters
quiz.explanation: Regularly checking progress lets you adjust before too much effort is wasted.

quiz.question: Can an "average" hide important differences in the numbers behind it?
choices: Yes, very different sets of numbers can share the same average
No, an average always tells the whole story
quiz.explanation: Averages can look identical while hiding very different underlying patterns.

slides.title: What is confirmation bias?
slides.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice and believe information that agrees with what you already think, while ignoring information that doesn't.

slides.title: Media literacy
slides.text: Understanding who created a piece of media, why, and who it's meant to persuade helps you judge how much to trust it.

slides.title: Common logical fallacies
slides.text: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning — like attacking a person instead of their argument, or assuming something is true just because 'everyone believes it.'

slides.title: Weighing evidence fairly
slides.text: Strong critical thinkers weigh the quality and quantity of evidence on all sides before forming a conclusion — not just picking whichever side feels more comfortable.

slides.title: Deciding under uncertainty
slides.text: Many real decisions have to be made without knowing everything for certain. Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not guaranteed ones, leads to better choices.

slides.title: Being willing to update
slides.text: Genuinely strong thinkers treat their own conclusions as open to revision — new, credible evidence should be able to change a well-reasoned mind.

slides.title: Steelmanning an argument
slides.text: Instead of attacking the weakest version of an opposing view, a strong thinker engages with the strongest, most reasonable version of it — called 'steelmanning.'

slides.title: Separating feelings from facts
slides.text: Recognizing when a strong emotional reaction — anger, excitement, fear — might be clouding a decision helps you think more clearly under pressure.

slides.title: Recognizing propaganda
slides.text: Propaganda uses one-sided, emotionally charged messaging to push a viewpoint rather than inform. Learning to notice it helps you separate persuasion from honest information.

slides.title: The scientific method, briefly
slides.text: Form a question, propose an explanation, test it, and revise based on results — this basic loop underlies careful thinking far beyond just science class.

quiz.question: What is confirmation bias?
choices: Favoring information that agrees with what you already believe
Always changing your opinion based on new facts
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias is a natural tendency to seek out agreeing information and dismiss disagreeing information.

quiz.question: What is a "logical fallacy"?
choices: A flaw in the structure or reasoning of an argument
Any statement that happens to be false
quiz.explanation: Logical fallacies are reasoning errors that can make even a false conclusion sound convincing.

quiz.question: What does "media literacy" involve?
choices: Understanding who made a piece of media and why
Watching as much media as possible without thinking about it
quiz.explanation: Media literacy is about critically evaluating the source and purpose behind media.

quiz.question: What does "steelmanning" an argument mean?
choices: Engaging with the strongest version of an opposing view
Ignoring opposing views entirely
quiz.explanation: Steelmanning means fairly addressing the best version of the other side's argument.

quiz.question: Why is deciding "under uncertainty" a real skill?
choices: Most real decisions don't come with guaranteed outcomes
Every decision in life comes with a guaranteed correct answer
quiz.explanation: Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not certainties, reflects how real decisions actually work.

quiz.question: Why might a strong emotional reaction be worth noticing during a decision?
choices: It might be clouding clear thinking in the moment
Emotions never affect decision-making at all
quiz.explanation: Recognizing strong emotions helps you separate how you feel from what the facts actually show.

quiz.question: Should a strong thinker be willing to change a conclusion?
choices: Yes, if credible new evidence supports it
No, changing your mind is always a weakness
quiz.explanation: Updating conclusions in light of solid new evidence is a hallmark of strong thinking, not weakness.

quiz.question: What is "propaganda"?
choices: One-sided, emotionally charged messaging meant to persuade
A neutral, balanced news report
quiz.explanation: Propaganda pushes a viewpoint through emotional persuasion rather than balanced information.

quiz.question: What is the basic loop of the scientific method?
choices: Question, propose an explanation, test it, revise based on results
Guess once and never check again
quiz.explanation: This loop of testing and revising ideas underlies careful thinking generally, not just science.

slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: When you feel happy, sad, or upset, saying it out loud with words helps people understand you better than yelling or crying alone.

slides.title: Listening matters too
slides.text: Talking is only half of communicating — really listening when someone else is talking is just as important.

slides.title: "Please" and "thank you"
slides.text: Saying please when you ask for something, and thank you when someone helps you, makes people happy to help you again.

slides.title: Asking for help
slides.text: If you're stuck or need something, asking for help with your words is a strong, smart thing to do — not something to feel bad about.

slides.title: Your face says a lot too
slides.text: A smile, a frown, or wide eyes all send a message, even before you say a single word.

slides.title: Taking turns talking
slides.text: Waiting for your turn to talk — instead of interrupting — helps everyone feel heard in a conversation.

slides.title: Naming your feelings
slides.text: Words like happy, sad, mad, and scared help you tell someone exactly what's going on inside you, instead of just crying or shouting.

slides.title: Showing what you mean
slides.text: If you can't find the words, pointing, drawing, or acting something out can help someone understand you too.

quiz.question: What helps people understand how you feel?
choices: Using your words to say it
Never saying anything at all
quiz.explanation: Putting feelings into words helps others understand and help you.

quiz.question: Is listening an important part of communicating?
choices: Yes, just as important as talking
No, only talking matters
quiz.explanation: Good communication is a two-way street — listening matters as much as talking.

quiz.question: When should you say "please"?
choices: When you're asking for something
Only on your birthday
quiz.explanation: "Please" is a polite way to ask for something.

quiz.question: If you're stuck and need help, what should you do?
choices: Ask for help with your words
Never tell anyone
quiz.explanation: Asking for help is a smart, strong choice, not something to be embarrassed about.

quiz.question: Can your face send a message, even without talking?
choices: Yes, like a smile or a frown
No, only words send messages
quiz.explanation: Facial expressions communicate feelings even before you say a word.

quiz.question: What are words like "happy" or "sad" used for?
choices: Naming your feelings so others understand
They have no real use
quiz.explanation: Feeling words help you tell someone exactly what's going on inside you.

quiz.question: If you can't find the words, what else can help you communicate?
choices: Pointing, drawing, or acting it out
Nothing else can ever help
quiz.explanation: Showing what you mean is a great backup when words are hard to find.

slides.title: What is active listening?
slides.text: Active listening means really paying attention — looking at the person, not interrupting, and thinking about what they're saying instead of just waiting for your turn to talk.

slides.title: Body language basics
slides.text: Crossed arms, a big smile, or looking away all send messages without any words — noticing body language helps you understand people better.

slides.title: Taking turns in conversation
slides.text: A good conversation feels like a back-and-forth game of catch, not one person talking the whole time.

slides.title: Disagreeing politely
slides.text: You can disagree with someone without being mean — saying 'I see it differently' is a respectful way to share a different opinion.

slides.title: Asking clarifying questions
slides.text: If you don't understand something someone said, asking 'can you explain that again?' is smarter than just pretending to understand.

slides.title: Written vs. spoken words

slides.title: Resolving a disagreement

slides.title: Written communication skills

slides.title: Speaking up in a group

slides.title: Writing a clear message

slides.title: Being kind online

slides.title: Your digital footprint

slides.title: Balancing screen time

slides.title: Your long-term digital footprint

slides.title: Healthy social media habits

slides.title: Reading privacy policies (a little)

slides.title: Digital wellbeing

slides.title: What is a problem?
slides.text: A problem is something that needs fixing — like a puzzle piece that won't fit, or a tower of blocks that keeps falling down.

slides.title: Try a different way
slides.text: If one way doesn't work, trying a different way is exactly what problem solvers do — like turning a puzzle piece around to see if it fits better.

slides.title: Mistakes are okay
slides.text: Making a mistake while trying to solve something isn't bad — it's actually a normal part of figuring things out.

slides.title: Asking for help is smart
slides.text: If you've tried and tried and still feel stuck, asking a grown-up or a friend for help is a smart next step, not giving up.

slides.title: Small steps first
slides.text: Breaking a big task, like cleaning a messy room, into small steps — like 'pick up the toys first' — makes it feel much less overwhelming.

slides.title: Celebrate figuring it out
slides.text: When you solve a problem — even a small one — it's worth feeling proud! You did real thinking to get there.

slides.title: Sorting and matching
slides.text: Matching socks into pairs or sorting blocks by color is a fun way to practice noticing what goes together — a real problem-solving skill.

slides.title: One step at a time

slides.title: Understanding the real problem

slides.title: Brainstorming ideas

slides.title: Trial and error

slides.title: Learning from what didn't work
slides.text: If a solution doesn't work, figuring out why helps you avoid making the same mistake again next time.

slides.title: Solving problems with others
slides.text: Sometimes two heads really are better than one — working with someone else can surface ideas you wouldn't have thought of alone.

slides.title: Taking a break when stuck
slides.text: Stepping away from a tricky problem for a few minutes sometimes helps your brain come back to it with a fresh idea.

slides.title: Comparing your solutions
slides.text: When you have more than one possible solution, thinking about which is easiest, fastest, or works best helps you choose wisely.

slides.title: Using tools to help

slides.title: Looking from a new angle
